docs.title: Pico Clock
docs.text:
A compact Raspberry Pi Pico W / Pico 2 W network clock with a bright display, automatic Wi‑Fi setup, and resilient time sync.

Built for a clean desk, a quiet wall, and a reliable time source that keeps itself online.

docs.title: Why it is useful
docs.text:
• Boots quickly and stays online on open Wi‑Fi networks.
  • Uses a captive-portal probe and NTP fallback logic to recover from flaky connectivity.
  • Tracks drift and latency so the time remains accurate over long sessions.
  • Shows the current time and optional date while keeping the display refresh loop lightweight.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
Easy setup

Flash the firmware, connect over serial, and configure the network and hostname in a few commands.

Reliable time sync

Uses IPv6-first NTP resolution with IPv4 fallback and retries against multiple servers.

Battery-friendly

The firmware separates networking work from display rendering so the UI loop can stay focused and responsive.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The clock exposes its configuration through the serial console. This keeps Wi‑Fi credentials and display preferences out of the firmware binary and lets you reconfigure the device in place.

docs.title: Wi‑Fi
docs.text:
wifi <ssid> [<password>]
  • Stores the SSID and optional password persistently.
  • If a network is open, the firmware will probe common captive-portal URLs as part of the connection check.
  • Password-protected networks are skipped for the portal probe.

docs.title: Hostname
docs.text:
hostname <name>

Set the device hostname. If no name is provided, the firmware resets the value to the default pico-clock hostname.

docs.title: Date display mode
docs.text:
date on|auto|off
  • on: always show the date beneath the time.
  • auto: only show the date around midnight.
  • off: keep the traditional time-only display.

showdate is accepted as an alias for compatibility.

docs.title: Example session
docs.text:
wifi OfficeWiFi mypassword
hostname kitchen-clock
date auto

After saving these settings, reboot the device or restart the networking flow to apply them.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the build environment
docs.text:
Install the toolchain and dependencies used by the repository:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y cmake gcc-arm-none-eabi libnewlib-arm-none-eabi build-essential

Then bootstrap the Pico SDK and local dependencies:

./scripts/bootstrap-pico.sh

Note

The project expects the Pico SDK under .deps/pico-sdk and the littlefs sources under .deps/littlefs.

docs.title: 2. Configure the firmware build
docs.text:
Use the default board target for a Pico 2 W build:

cmake -S . -B build -DPICO_SDK_PATH=$PWD/.deps/pico-sdk -DPICO_BOARD=pico2_w

To target a Pico W instead:

cmake -S . -B build -DPICO_SDK_PATH=$PWD/.deps/pico-sdk -DPICO_BOARD=pico_w

docs.title: 3. Build the firmware
docs.text:
cmake --build build -j2

The generated build outputs are written to build/ as .uf2, .elf, .bin, and .hex artifacts.

docs.title: 4. Flash and test the device
docs.text:
1. Put the Pico into USB bootloader mode.
  2. Copy the generated .uf2 image to the mounted drive.
  3. Open the serial console at the configured baud rate.
  4. Configure the Wi‑Fi network and hostname as needed.

docs.title: 5. Configure the device over serial
docs.text:
After the first boot, configure the device with serial commands:

wifi <ssid> [<password>]
hostname <name>
date on|auto|off

Example:

wifi GuestNetwork secretpass
hostname desk-clock
date auto

The wifi command stores the credentials persistently. The hostname and date commands control the device identity and date display behaviour.

docs.title: Missing Pico SDK or LittleFS sources
docs.text:
If configuration fails because the Pico SDK or lfs.c is absent, prepare the project dependencies first:

./scripts/bootstrap-pico.sh

If the build still complains about missing lfs.c, clone the littlefs dependency manually:

mkdir -p .deps
git -C .deps clone --depth 1 https://github.com/littlefs-project/littlefs.git littlefs

docs.title: Device does not connect to Wi‑Fi
docs.text:
• Confirm the wifi command was stored correctly.
  • Check the serial console for the active SSID and the network state.
  • Ensure the network is open or uses a supported password flow.
  • Reboot the Pico after changing the configuration.

docs.title: Time is wrong
docs.text:
• Verify that NTP is reachable over the network.
  • Check that the device has a valid gateway and DNS path.
  • Look at the serial logs for drift and latency values; they are reported as part of the runtime loop.

docs.title: Display shows the wrong behaviour
docs.text:
• Use date on|auto|off to toggle the date visibility.
  • Check that the hostname is set correctly.
  • Confirm the framebuffer is updating after the board boots.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
wifi <ssid> [<password>]
hostname <name>
date on|auto|off

If the issue persists, use the serial output during startup to track the networking and sync stages.
